item.title: From Individual Transaction to Social Climate
item.lead: This document addresses digital intimacy not as isolated consumer behavior, but as a potential factor in how people learn to interpret each other.

blocks.text: A central idea is conditioning. When a user repeatedly experiences that attention is for sale, this can, according to the document, alter expectations about other relationships. Similarly, someone who works as a salesperson for years can learn to assess every interaction based on time, risk, or revenue. This creates a dual transformation: both buyer and seller begin to view the other through a commercial lens.

The source refers to this as the "customer service syndrome" in human relationships. This concept is not a clinical diagnosis, but a metaphor for a learning process in which social interaction is evaluated based on efficiency, delivery expectation, and yield.

The sociological implication is significant. Social norms are not merely laws; they also arise from repeated interaction. When digital platforms increasingly absorb hours of social attention, their transactional logic can be carried beyond the interface. This document suggests that precisely this spillover effect should be investigated.

The question, therefore, is not only how many people consume digital intimacy, but what expectations they thereby develop about what another person "owes," how quickly a response should come, and how much emotional attention is reasonably expected for free.
